潘汉年.note: 1906–1977. A literary man turned master of CCP intelligence and united-front work; deputy head of the Social Affairs Department, working from Hong Kong and Shanghai. Wrongly imprisoned as an “inner traitor” in 1955; rehabilitated in 1982.

张国焘.note: 1897–1979. A founder of the CCP and commander of the Fourth Front Army; Mao Zedong’s chief rival on the Long March. Defected to the Nationalists in 1938; later emigrated and died in Canada.

胡宗南.note: 1896–1962. Chiang Kai-shek’s favored Whampoa protégé and senior commander in the northwest, the “King of the Northwest”; his forces blockaded the Border Region and took Yan’an in 1947.

周兴.note: 1905–1975. Head of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region Security Office (the “Border Security”) through the Yan’an years; later a deputy minister of public security.

徐恩曾.note: 1896–1985. Head of the Nationalist Zhongtong; a nephew-by-marriage of Chen Guofu and a member of the “CC Clique.” His memoir is quoted throughout this book.

陈立夫.note: 1900–2001. Nationalist party boss who, with his brother Chen Guofu, led the “CC Clique”; founding director of the bureaus that became Zhongtong and Juntong.

王明.note: 1904–1974. Leader of the Moscow-trained “28 Bolsheviks” and the CCP’s representative to the Comintern; a rival to Mao whose successive “Left” and “Right” lines the author disparages.

中央社会部.note: The CCP’s central intelligence and security organ from February 1939, headed by Kang Sheng; known within the Party as 中社部 (Zhongshebu). The bland name “Social Affairs” was itself a cover.

陕甘宁边区保安处.note: The Border Region government’s combined public-security and procuratorial organ, known for short as 边保 (Bianbao, the “Border Security”); the executing arm of Communist security work in Yan’an, and outwardly the government face of the Northwest Bureau’s Social Affairs Department.

ch02.note: A jimao xin (鸡毛信), or “chicken-feather letter”: an urgent dispatch with one or more chicken feathers fastened to it, the feathers signalling that it was to be carried at top speed, day and night, changing runners as needed. The device was old and widespread in rural China and became a staple of Communist wartime lore.

The Laoshan Incident (劳山事件) of 25 April 1937, in which bandits ambushed Zhou Enlai’s convoy in the hills south of Yan’an. Zhou’s adjutant Chen Youcai, dressed in a Western suit as a decoy, was killed; the ambushers took him for the important man and found Zhou’s calling cards on the body. The account is broadly corroborated. Two small internal discrepancies in the source are worth noting: its photo caption dates the affair 24 April against the 25th given in the text, and it twice names the ambush site “Yanqiushan” (沿湫山) while calling the affair after Laoshan.

Deng Xiaoping, Mao Zetan (Mao Zedong’s younger brother), Xie Weijun, and Gu Bo, four cadres of the Jiangxi Soviet condemned together in 1933 as followers of a “Luo Ming line” and punished for their closeness to Mao Zedong, who was then out of power. All but Deng Xiaoping died within a few years; Deng’s later rehabilitation and rise are among the ironies the author leaves unspoken.

The Gelaohui (哥老会), a sworn-brotherhood secret society widespread in the Chinese countryside from the nineteenth century. Belonging to neither party, such societies commanded real local loyalty and armed men, and both Nationalists and Communists by turns courted and feared them.

The Lixingshe (力行社, “Vigorous Action Society”) was the secret inner core of the Chinese Renaissance Society, popularly the “Blue Shirts,” a militarist, nationalist body founded in 1932 by Whampoa officers loyal to Chiang Kai-shek and often likened to the fascist movements of the day. Its Special Services Department under Dai Li grew into the military secret service later called Juntong.

Japan a passing skin ailment, the Communists a disease in the heart and vitals (疥癣之患 / 心腹大患): the metaphor recurs in accounts of Chiang Kai-shek’s strategic priorities and captures the weight he gave the internal enemy over the invader. The exact wording varies among sources; the sense is well attested.

The “three-in-one” (三位一体) alignment of late 1936 joined the Communists, Zhang Xueliang’s Northeast Army, and Yang Hucheng’s Northwestern Army in a common front in the northwest, the coalition behind the Xi’an Incident. With Zhang detained and Yang forced abroad afterward and their armies moved away, it dissolved, leaving the Communists without their two military partners, as the author says.

ch02.anchor: The heavy work of the military blockade fell to Hu Zongnan
ch02.note: Hu Zongnan (1896–1962), Chiang Kai-shek’s favored Whampoa protégé and the senior Nationalist commander in the northwest, nicknamed the “King of the Northwest.” From 1939 the bulk of his large force blockaded and menaced the Border Region rather than fighting Japan, a diversion of strength the Communists never forgot; in 1947 his troops briefly captured Yan’an.

At the Crossroads (三岔口, Sanchakou) is a celebrated Peking-opera scene in which two men fight in total darkness, each blind to the other, their groping mock-combat performed in full stage light. The image, of allies and enemies grappling in the dark on the same ground, is the author’s figure for the tangled traffic of the blockade years.

ch02.anchor: the new climate of "reform and opening"
ch02.note: The author writes literally “the new situation of reform and opening” (改革开放), the fixed slogan for the era of economic liberalization that began in 1978, some four decades after these events. The anachronism is his own, a playful borrowing: the united front “opened” the sealed Nationalist-Communist front, and that opening, he suggests, only multiplied the covert contest. It is in no sense a term of the 1930s.

ch02.anchor: swore to be loyal to Marshal Mao
ch02.note: Xu Shiyou (1906–1985), a hot-tempered general of the Fourth Front Army, trained as a boy at the Shaolin monastery and later a senior PLA commander. The story of Mao Zedong disarming his rage by handing him a loaded pistol is often told, and stands for Mao’s careful winning-over of the Fourth Front Army cadres after Zhang Guotao’s fall.

ch02.anchor: The tomb of the Yellow Emperor, Xuanyuan
ch02.note: The Mausoleum of the Yellow Emperor at Huangling honors the legendary ancestor of the Chinese people and is a national shrine; sacrifices there at Qingming, the tomb-sweeping festival, are an old imperial rite revived to invoke national unity. At the joint Nationalist-Communist sacrifice of April 1938 Mao Zedong composed a sacrificial ode, a set-piece of the united-front moment.

Zhang Guotao (1897–1979), a founder of the CCP and commander of the powerful Fourth Front Army, had been Mao Zedong’s chief rival for leadership on the Long March; his bid failed and his army was broken. The Yan’an criticism recounted here drove his defection to the Nationalists in April 1938, which ended his Communist career; he later emigrated and died in Canada. That not even his bodyguard would follow him is the author’s pointed detail.

ch02.anchor: better to kill a thousand by mistake than let one slip through
ch02.note: A byword for the Nationalist white terror against Communists from 1927 on. The 1929 “Communist Surrender Law” and its fanxingyuan (反省院, “houses of reflection,” or repentance houses), detention centers meant to make captured Communists recant, marked a shift from mass killing to the subtler policy of turning prisoners, which, as the author notes, produced the very turncoats who later staffed the Nationalist services.

ch02.anchor: one cannot avoid speaking of this Kang Sheng
ch02.note: This unusually harsh portrait of Kang Sheng (1898–1975) reflects the verdict reached after his death. Once the CCP’s intelligence and security chief, he became the driving figure of the Yan’an “Rescue Campaign” (see Chapter 9) and, decades later, a chief instrument of the Cultural Revolution’s persecutions. He died laden with honors, but in 1980 the Party posthumously expelled him and withdrew his eulogy. The author’s open contempt is itself striking in a book so sympathetic to most of its subjects.

ch02.anchor: Dong Biwu, Lin Boqu, Xie Juezai, and Xu Teli
ch02.note: By custom only a handful of the Yan’an leadership, revered for their age and seniority, were addressed as “Elder.” These four, together with Wu Yuzhang, were known as the “Five Elders of Yan’an” (延安五老). That the much younger Kang Sheng could claim the title is the author’s sardonic point.

Pan Hannian’s fall came in 1955: arrested as an “inner traitor,” he was imprisoned for having concealed a secret wartime meeting with the collaborationist Wang Jingwei. He died in disgrace in 1977 and was rehabilitated in 1982, as the author records. The case is among the best-known miscarriages of the Maoist security system, and the sympathy here is that of his old comrades of the Special Branch.

“Snow” (沁园春·雪, to the tune Qinyuanchun), Mao Zedong’s most famous poem, written in the winter of 1936 after the Long March reached northern Shaanxi; surveying the snow-bound land, it moves to a sweeping claim on China’s history and future. Its publication in Chongqing in 1945, during the peace talks, caused a sensation.
